Reasons for thanking the Lord for the divine mercies granted in 1879: the Church's recognition of the Family of Saint Anne; the foundation of new Houses, also in America; the service to the poor of Piacenza; the considerable number of vocations: 57 sisters received the habit, a number reduced by the hardship of the times, since the Mother House could not receive young women without a dowry. Recommendations to Superiors and Sisters. Notice of the deceased Sisters to be prayed for.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughters,

  1. Our Institute, the family of the August and glorious Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate our Mother, has now entered the fourteenth year of its existence, a year we hope will be one of great glory for it, as was the year just ended.

  2. Yes, Daughters, very many are the divine mercies with which the year 1879 was filled. The greatest, most heartfelt and splendid is that Holy Church, through her Vicar, now Leo XIII, has definitively recognised our family as a Religious family, which is to say a family of God.1

  3. This approval was welcomed, since it leaves not the slightest doubt that those who gather in it find all the means to reach that eminent holiness to which God calls those who make special profession of the evangelical counsels of poverty, obedience and chastity.2

  4. As a result we see the peoples' sympathy ever growing towards us, who bear the most noble name of Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, and so we are certain that this name, the most honourable for a creature, we did not take for ourselves, but it was imposed on us by heaven.3

  1. A clear sign of this sympathy is the many requests received for founding houses in various places. The foundations agreed number 19, nine of which have already opened and the other ten will open shortly.4 Among these new houses one has been founded in America, in Bolivia, beside the one already there.5 In it some 80 girls of ours are being educated in religion. Negotiations are under way to found, likewise there in America, three more houses in three different cities,6 to which 40 Sisters would be called.

  2. This eagerness to have our Sisters arises from seeing the fine results obtained by the peoples who have them, both in hospitals and in schools.

  3. One of the benefits the Lord is pleased to bestow on His creatures through our Sisters, and which deserves special mention, is the distribution of soup to the poor. In this winter of seventy-nine and eighty the Lord is punishing the sins of the world with cold and hunger.7 Well, His mercy, which is never separated from His divine justice, has called us, His ministers, to relieve so many wretched people, giving them food and clothing every day. In the Mother House alone some three thousand beggars are fed daily with good, well-seasoned soup.8

  4. What a great grace this is, Sisters! What a sign of predilection the Lord gives us! The way to thank Him for such distinction is to humble ourselves before His divine Majesty, sincerely acknowledging our unworthiness, and to work unsparingly to carry out so noble an office.

  5. The number clothed was 57, far fewer than in '78; but the reason was not a shortage of postulants asking to wear the habit of the Holy Mother; it was that, in these critical times, they could not bring the required dowry, small as it is. On the other hand the Mother House, given the hardship of the times, could not open its arms to receive them without a dowry.

  1. And here we must urge thrift, especially on the Superiors, so that after feeding and clothing the Sisters they can send any surplus to the Mother House.

  2. They are bound to this by love, by vow and by justice. By love: they must know that the fruitfulness of the Institute

depends on two things: the first is that the Lord call many, even with a very small dowry or none. Now this year the first was not lacking, for the requests were very many, but the Mother House lacked the means to receive them without a dowry. And on whom does it depend that the Mother House has these means? It depends precisely on the thrift of the Superiors.

  1. It is consoling to say that many true Daughters of the Holy Mother, eager to see her family spread throughout the world, are most careful to account for every penny, as the saying goes, so as to have surplus to send to the Mother House, knowing that the well-being of the whole Institute springs from its well-being.9 The Mother House is the heart of the Institute; if the heart is healthy and full of life, the members in the other Houses are also healthy and strong.

  2. But the Holy Mother does not receive this joy from all. There are some spendthrifts who, despite generous allowances, never have anything to save. They are unloving and unnatural, caring nothing for the Institute's glory. Besides not10 being unloving towards the Institute, they risk failing in justice by harming it, for let them remember that they are not owners of the goods of the Houses they head, but simply administrators.

  3. It is worth noting that, just as Superiors who love the Institute and take care not to squander its goods also treat their sisters well, loving them when healthy and caring for them when sick, so those who live only for themselves and cannot save neglect their sisters and make them go short of food and clothing.

  4. We must also again impress on some Superiors that they should beware of fearing that the sisters will write to the Mother about them: this fear springs from duplicity, for simple-hearted Superiors like to be known by their Mother so as to be helped to advance in virtue and free themselves of faults.

  5. But these Superiors say: "We do not mind people writing to the Mother about our doings, but we do mind their writing falsehoods and slander". A frivolous pretext, dictated by their pride and arrogance. Humility loves to resemble Jesus Christ, who for love of us chose to submit to being slandered. This pretext, moreover, wrongs the [higher] Superiors, treating them as imprudent and rash, unable to weigh the reports they receive against Superiors so as to tell the false from the true.11

  6. And if now and then the Lord permits Superiors to be deceived, this serves to bring out all the more the innocence of the one slandered, and afterwards the Lord uses her to do great good for His glory.

  7. A Superior who fears and resents the sisters writing to the Mother is utterly unworthy of being one, and once the Superiors discover this base and dishonourable sin in her, she must be inexorably removed from office.

  8. Let us now consider the sisters' duty towards their Superiors. The sisters must have eyes to see their Superiors' wishes, to receive them reverently and carry them out promptly, to see the duty of the office laid on them, whether as nurse or in school, etc., etc., and fulfil it faithfully; but they must be blind so as not to pry into and investigate their Superiors' conduct.12

  9. Here perhaps the difficulty will arise in their minds: "but the rule does require the sisters to inform the Mother of serious faults in their superiors". How can we fulfil this duty if we do not observe them?

  10. Sisters, Superiors are like the sun, which, being on high, cannot hide its large spots that eclipse it from anyone not wholly without eyes. So it is with the grave faults of Superiors that ruin their souls and scandalise their subjects; these faults are necessarily seen by the sisters even with their eyes closed.

  11. All see if she wickedly goes out of her way to speak alone with persons of the other sex; all see if through lukewarmness she neglects works of piety; all see if she does not follow the Mother House in providing her Community with food and clothing, or if she is not a mother to the sick. So let the sisters love their Superiors with a sincere love, a filial love, a love that is reverent, humble and obedient, and then they will always find them good.

  12. We end this letter by noting the number of sisters the Holy Mother added to her crown last year. I mean those fortunate sisters who have reached the one supreme end for which they joined the Institute, which is to die the death of the just, the death precious in God's sight, a death that has nothing fearful but its name; for in reality it is only a passage from misery to happiness, from suffering to enjoyment, from humiliation to eternal glory. These favoured ones numbered 15. The sisters are asked for the customary prayers for the dead. Urging you, dearest daughters, to profit by these counsels, we implore the Lord's Blessing upon you, and remain in the sacred hearts of Jesus and Mary and of the Holy Mother your affectionate

Giov. Batta. Tornatore Miss. M. Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

The Superior for the new house at Pisa will arrive. Let her accompany her and organise everything, instructing her and the Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Listen, you will receive this letter from Sr. A. Ancilla; she is coming to be Superior at Pisa, where on Thursday you will telegraph the Parish Priest and tell him the time of your arrival.1 He writes that I should first send two to organise the House.

  2. So I have thought of doing this: you will go with her and when everything is in order you will telegraph me to send the others. As for the others, for the money tell the Parish Priest that when I have sent them I will send him the whole account, so he will see what has been spent.2

  3. Stay until they are well settled; I urge you to instruct her well, teach her, and you will be able to tell me whether she is good and doing well;3 likewise Sr. A. Cipriana, who comes with her;4 she is one of those going to Pisa, an angel in the flesh, and meanwhile, staying in Pistoia, she will go a little to the sick and learn to pull teeth, which I am sure she will do very well. Tell me something as soon as you are in that house. Do you understand? Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

She is glad of the good news of the Community. She asks for a Sister for a few days. Two others will come to her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am glad of what you tell me about the Sisters; truly I can say it is my only consolation when I hear that all is well and the Sisters are behaving well.

  2. Now I would really like you to do me the kindness of lending me Sr. A. Reparata for a few days;1 I have to open a hospital and would need her by Thursday2; I hope she will be here, won't she?3 And I will send you Sr. A. Sabina with another one provisionally, and then return Reparata to you. So do me this favour. On Thursday I will expect her on the 2 p.m. train, and that same day I will send you the other two. Goodbye, yours for ever,

affectionate M. Rosa

She sends the receipt for the shipment of the case. Letters are not arriving; she sends this L by registered post. She hopes order and peace will be restored under the new President. She explains how to send the payment for the cloth she bought and sent. Various news from Piacenza and a request for news. She will send the circular letter at the end of the month.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

  1. I received your letter dated 3 November on 31 January 1880. I hear you never receive the case and would like to know the name of the steamer; I am sending you the insurance document, you will see everything;1 I have already sent you another registered letter and you never acknowledge receipt. I do not know what to think; I always send you everything registered and never see that you receive it. Let us hope you will.

  2. I hope it is all over, for I hear they have made another president, is it true?2 How I have suffered! Enough, I look forward to your telling me about it. Because of this I hope there will be no more revolution, for surely everything will have been settled.

  3. As for the rest, for sending me what you mention,3 Gaspare had written to you how to do it, but I see you never receive these blessed letters, which would be the safest way; then I could pay for the cloth I sent you; not wanting to wait any longer, I had to pay for ours, which came to a fine sum, and yours is 1600 f,4 plus shipping costs; so enclosed you will find again the person to whom you should hand them, a banker who then remits them by draft to this one in Piacenza, and then we get them at once; that is how you should do it.

  4. I hear about Sr. A. Clelia. If you thought her capable, she could come back saying she is coming to fetch the others, and then I would send another; what do you think?5 Do as you think best, and the Lord will see to it, for surely the Holy Mother will not allow her to go her own way; she will set her right!

  5. So one of you must come sooner or later, for I hear you are taking postulants, and when you have 8 or 10 who have done 6 or 8 months of novitiate they will have to come here; that way you will have more room to make some changes; what do you think?

  6. I would like to hear that you are a little stronger and sturdier and back to how you were, in short, robust.6 It is very cold here and, worse, there is great hunger. If you saw how many soups are given out you would not believe it.7 At Cortemaggiore too they give out as many.

  7. For two days there has been a little sun and the cold is easing. I am still in Piacenza and cannot leave until the end of February because I have an immense amount to do. I hope that before you receive this you will have received all the others, including the registered ones.

  8. At the end of this month I will send you the circular we are printing;8 I have also written to all the sisters, and in one of yours, which could not be properly understood, you seemed to say that Sr. A. Lucia has died, is it true? I do not know how to take it, you tell me nothing;9 I also wrote to Father Rocchi and to the Bishop [by] the other post.

  9. I hope the war will end and then letters will no longer go astray, for from what I see a good number have been lost; clearly there is confusion, but what grieves me most is the big case of cloth that has gone missing. Let us hope not! I would like you to write to me as soon as you receive this. Oh! if a telegram did not cost so much, how gladly I would receive one! Enough. You will do what you think best.

  1. Now let us talk a little about observance, and let us hope it always flourishes in America as, by God's mercy, it does in this House and in all those of Upper and Lower Italy.10 From the circular you will see the faults that prevail in the houses, especially that of disposing of the Institute's goods and taking the liberty of giving them to relatives, and likewise the letters they write; enough, you will read it.

  2. I hope the Sisters have settled down well and that peace reigns. I have also written to Sr. A. Rosa.11 In this one I am not writing to anyone; in another I will answer all the sisters who write to me. Goodbye, yours for all ages affectionate M. Rosa

She consoles her on her brother's sudden death. May prayer and reflection help her benefit the soul of the deceased and find peace herself.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear of your grief with great sorrow,1 but you must reflect that we are made for this end, and besides, a dear daughter of Saint Anne must think of praying and of being able to help that soul.2

  2. Oh! daughter, think that in your position you can help him with holy resignation and prayers, Holy Communion, Mass every day. How could my daughter, so gifted with intelligence, let herself be cast down by such useless sadness?3 Reason, time and reflection are the only things that bring peace.

  3. Sure that my daughter will do so, I hold you close in the heart of Jesus, where I hope you will find everything, including peace, and be content; and believe me

your affectionate M. Rosa

Her letters have not arrived; she has sent several, some registered. She suggests how and what to say to the Sisters about her instructions and admonitions. They need gentleness. She urges her to write to the Bishop of Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. You want letters and tell me that for several days you have received none; they must have gone astray; besides, I have sent you several by registered post, especially those containing the receipts for the case, and I sent another registered one about 8 days ago. Now I keep a record of them1 and I assure you I always write, I never miss a post.

  2. Listen, would it not be good if in the chapters2 you hold, speaking gently and kindly, you said: "Daughters, do not be scandalised if you see me give something extra or make some difference for someone;3 do not think I love her more! No, to me you are all my dearest sisters, and I assure you that if at times I urge you to take courage and not fear evil so much, it is because I know the ground I am testing is good, and by sometimes going deep to the roots4 the virtues stand out all the more. For the rest, bear with me too in many things if you find me too stern; but I assure you that one day you will see that my firmness was only to make you grow in virtue".

  3. Believe me, daughter, our dear daughters are children and also need a little petting.

For pity's sake, let favouritism never enter your community, for it would be the plague.5 But knowing you well enough, I know how fair you are; I do not doubt this at all.

4. Write, I repeat, to the Bishop here in Piacenza; you should have done so before, for it really would have been your duty.

For now I add nothing; I would only like to hear that you are strong, robust and healed of your infirmities,6 while I call myself yours for all ages affectionate M. Rosa

She praises her for starting the new house at Pisa. She awaits more consoling news.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. Your letter was a real consolation amid countless sorrows!2 well done, well done; may God continue to give you His holy light and you to respond to it.

  2. So the Pisa house is open; now we must see to consolidating it. Well, now it is up to you to see that instead of 4, who are no use at all,3 there are at least 6 or 8; it seems to me that with the salary they have they can manage very well, and I will send the alms-collectors,4 for I have two really good ones.

  3. I await your letters; write to me often, for they are a real consolation. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

She shares her grief and invites her to resignation and prayer.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I share as much as I can and know all your grief, but! one thing holds me back, and that is holy resignation!2 Listen, my dear daughter, I have been through all these sorrows and more: my son! and a father, a brother, but! resigned! and only in holy resignation did I find comfort.3

2. I threw myself into the heart of Jesus, I had recourse to the Crucified, and in Him, my dear, oh! I always found everything.4

Try it and you will see.5 I leave you in the heart of Jesus6 and call myself your affectionate M. Rosa

Advice. She urges her to be cheerful.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear of your troubles and make them mine; send the girl away at once, for one can spoil all the others. Have her accompanied by the two alms-collectors or by others you think fit.1

  2. I understood little of your letter;2 I only tell you to keep your spirits up and be cheerful; after the storm comes fair weather.

Goodbye, thank you for the basket3 your affectionate M. Rosa

She tells her of her coming departure. She asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received yours with the statement enclosed,1 and so I hear the many good items of news. God willing, at the end of this [month] I shall leave Piacenza. I do not know when I shall reach Rome, because I must stop in many places.2 Pray and have others pray that I may have a good journey, and believe me

your affectionate M. Rosa

She informs her of her coming departure from Piacenza.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. God willing, next Wednesday2 I shall set out, but first I have to visit two houses and then I will go to Pistoia; I will telegraph you before leaving the last house.

  2. You have done everything well; I approve it all.3 We shall talk better in person. Goodbye, I am your

affectionate M. Rosa

I greet everyone and am

She gives her opinion on accepting a postulant.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received a letter from a certain Diega Corso of your Orphanage, who would like to be accepted among the Daughters of Saint Anne. If you think she is truly good like the other one I accepted, tell her she is accepted like the other.

  2. See that they have at least the fare for the journey1 and then you will bring her to me in Naples with the other. Goodbye, yours for ever

affectionate M. Rosa

She explains how to overcome her doubts about confession and what principles to follow to benefit from it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am so busy that I do not know how to answer your letter.1 I will only tell you that we must hold firmly to [what] Holy Mother Church has taught us: that to make a good and holy confession we must aim at nothing but intense sorrow for our sins and earnest resolutions to amend, and look at nothing else.

  2. If you do this, be sure you will be dear to the heart of Jesus, in the lively hope of amending all your faults, making earnest promises never to fall back, keeping the Holy Rules and asking God for holy perseverance. Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me always

your affectionate M. Rosa

She authorises the work on the house. She has received the money order.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Courage, then, and never mistrust that dear Jesus who does everything for our good. I have written to Cimatti to go ahead with certain works.1 I received the money order and have already handed everything over; if you can, send the rest; if not, I will make it up.2 You ought to send me something of the half-year accounts3 of that house. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

Alarmed at what she has written about the Superior of the Pisa house, she proposes two solutions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received your letter1 and hear that you have already begun the nursing, but the news of that sister who was to be superior — this way she behaves — hurts me deeply;2 so, since Jesus has let us know her, we must at once try to put it right.

  2. This is what we will do: send her to Pistoia and bring Sr. A. Geronima, whom you left in your place, to you, and make her vice-superior; then you can go straight to Pistoia and put your little affairs in order, and I will not be long in coming, for God willing I shall leave next Saturday,3 but I must stop at two houses and then I shall be with you, for I see the sisters have little affection for this superior.4

  3. If, however, you think she could continue, then we will do this: read her these two lines I put at the foot of this letter; you must leave her as vice-superior. She will be able to do nothing without your consent, and you will go there every month, receive the alms-collectors' money and leave her only what is strictly necessary, and she will be vice-superior.5

  4. Meanwhile I am writing to her, so she will calm down, and the sisters too, and everything will be settled.

Tomorrow, God willing, I hope to send you two sisters. Goodbye; much more in person your affectionate M. Rosa

She reassures her by relieving her of the office of Superior pending her visit, now imminent.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I gather from your letter that you are not very happy;1 well then, we will do this: provisionally, until I arrive, you will remain vice-superior and Sr. A. Crocifissa Superior, and when she goes to Pisa2 you will take her orders and abide by what she tells you. Be cheerful, for in a few days I shall be there. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

She appoints her Superior and explains how she should handle the administration. She will send her a Sister teacher as soon as possible.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. So, pay close attention: in the name of my beloved Jesus, listen to me, act, and obey exactly. This is what we will do: you will remain Superior, and when you go collecting alms Sr. A. Colomba will take your place,1 and I hope you will do well and I shall have no cause for sorrow.

  2. Now to financial matters: I will send you all the books,2 where you will see what you must collect and the money I hold.

  3. As for the teaching certificate, I will do everything to prevent a little lay teacher being brought in too soon,3 but for the moment I do not know what to do; meanwhile you have a certificate there and can say so; you must send it by registered post with 5 seals to Invorio Inferiore at once, and I will do everything to send you another.4

  4. I assure you I am very, very anxious, but I hope you will be well and find a way out. I really do not know whom to send you for the alms-collecting; enough, let us hope.5

Goodbye, your affectionate. Do not come yourself, for it would be useless. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

P.S. As for the girl for service, the Count does not want her, so you need not send her to be trained; there is no need for her to go.6

She thanks her and asks for prayers.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. Thank you for what you do for me;2 as for doubting that the Most Holy Virgin will grant me the grace — oh!3 that is too much! Enough, pray and have others pray! Thank you for the potatoes. As for the Postulants, do as you say.

Goodbye, yours in my dear Crucified One affectionate M. Rosa

By the end of next week I shall be in Florence.

She orders her to leave at once for Pisa, where Sr. A. Crocifissa is waiting to instruct her about the house and the work.1

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. As soon as you receive this letter, without saying anything to anyone, anyone at all, take your things and leave for Pisa, where Sr. A. Crocifissa is waiting for you and will install you as Superior of that house.2

  2. I repeat, say nothing to anyone and leave right away for Pisa, because that Superior3 has been removed to open a new house.

  3. You are changing for the better: first, you will be closer to Rome and we shall be able to see each other more often; second, because it is a lovely little house and you will be very, very happy there.

  4. So we are agreed; go at once, at once, for Sr. A. Crocifissa is waiting for you and will instruct you in everything and tell you how to proceed. In the firm confidence that you will obey blindly, holding you close to my dear Crucified One, I call myself yours for ever

affectionate M. Rosa G.

Please leave at once without objections.

She urges observance of the Rules: let her put an end to grumbling and to listening to insinuations. She clarifies the scope of her task.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I read your two letters just as I arrived from Pistoia,2 after suffering horribly, but always gladly, for I know that suffering alone is good for my soul. So you flee from it! and you are my daughter! it cannot be! the most beautiful and sweet comfort is loving Jesus!

  2. Oh! ill-starred tongues that fall upon your papier-mâché heart, sacrilegious grumblings and, worse still, diabolical vipers.3 What good have the Father's sermons done?4 You tell me: either she goes or I go; why such fury?5 Oh! you say you love a poor Mother, but what can I say? I must say I do not believe it.

  3. Let me give vent to my thoughts, for if that were so it seems to me you should not act like this; first you would keep our holy Rules by putting an end to grumbling — first by not listening to it at all, so as to set an example to the others; besides, you would not feel your heart wounded by muddled6 words reported to you, for whoever speaks in passion never tells the truth.

  4. So you must realise that as soon as you mention to the Mother the girls and anything that is wrong, which you see with your own eyes, she will certainly not be slow to remedy it; but these are not rifle shots!7

  5. As for her, I tell you she should have little or nothing to do with you; it is enough that she does not prevent you from doing your job and treats you well; otherwise there is nothing to be done.8

  6. I cannot understand, regarding the linen, if it happened that she gave you others' linen, which I do not believe, for you will see for yourself.9

  7. Listen, in two months I shall be back and will come; your wish will be granted; meanwhile look after yourself, for pity's sake.

  8. Accepting the girls depends on the superior, but that one is an illegitimate child who can be accepted, for she is not one of those who count among the foundlings.10 Goodbye, I am unwell and find it hard to write.

Goodbye your affectionate M. Rosa

1. In April the Mother was not in Pistoia. From the text of this letter and of the two it answers, it is from March.

An alms-collecting Sister must be transferred to Piacenza. Let her see to it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1, I hear with no little surprise what happened to the two alms-collectors;1 so this cannot be all; other consequences would follow.2

2. So it is time to take her away from Genoa; send her to Piacenza at once, and you can go collecting yourself; and God willing, on my return from Rome I will come and then we can...3

Enough, I am overwhelmed with work,

your affectionate M. Rosa

She tells her to send two Sisters to Ferrara, with the relevant explanations.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Listen, I need you to send Sr. A. Ulderica to Ferrara at once, provisionally, with the alms-collector who will have arrived from Sestri, called Sr.2 A. Ferdinanda? If she has not arrived, then let Sr. A. Gabriella go with Sr. A. Ulderica, and send them to Ferrara on the 1.40 through train; one obedience paper made out to Ferrara is enough.3 At once, at once, because I need them to be in Ferrara tomorrow evening.

  2. I am not continuing in my own hand because I must go out, and tomorrow I leave for Florence;4 I will expect letters there.

The Lord bless you, most affectionate Mother Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

P.S. Tell them that as soon as they reach Bologna they should look for the Ferrara train straight away.

  • Send some large sacks here at once to be filled with chestnuts and potatoes.

  • Sr. A. Gabriella does not need a bundle,5 the others do.

She announces the arrival of the new Superior and her own.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. When Sr. A. Antonietta1 arrives, do not say anything to her about her being Superior. Wait for me first; when I come we will do everything.

  2. Today I expected letters from you telling me something about the house there.2

Goodbye; on Sunday [I shall leave] on the 5 p.m. train and arrive at half past 7. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

She praises her obedience, the virtue that leads to the perfection of love. She urges her to love, pray and act only out of love, accepting suffering. She gives her various tasks. Advice. News.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

  1. Your telegram was a real consolation to me, showing your obedience. Oh! blessed are you if you know how to practise this beautiful virtue well; it is the only one that serves us to advance on the way of perfection and obtain the love of God!2

  2. Dear Francesca, this alone can be the delight and contentment of your heart; this is our only sure, unchanging, eternal good; all the rest is deceptive, perishable and fleeting.

  3. You alone, my Good, are the unchanging one, the only good that can make our love happy.3

  4. Yes, my dear daughter, love, love Jesus alone! May the dear eternal Father be your joy,4 St Michael the Archangel your guide. Ask him to watch over your actions so that they may be acceptable to the good God!

  5. Oh! dear daughter! if you knew how sweet the love of God is! A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Here I am with you again, though I must leave in a few hours. Listen, a postulant will come to you from Parma; she must have all her papers and things and two thousand L. (2000); I have agreed that she will never go to the sick, so never send her.

  2. At the end of this month you and Beppa will go for a day to Arena Po to Sr. A. Berta to do her accounts for submission; have a look and then tell me. She has a girl and asked me to keep her on permanently;1 I said no; please observe everything carefully.

  3. Your letter, which I received last night, was a real consolation, because Gaspare always tells me Carla is unwell.2

  4. Now about Checco:3 since he has to sit his examinations in Bologna, give him the address of the room we keep there4 and tell him he can have his lunch made there and can bring something, such as salami and wine, for breakfast.

You too should write to those sisters;5 you can write to your mother about it, though I have already told her something. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

She orders her to send two Sisters.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. So send Sr. A. Natalina and Sr. A. Emma as soon as you can.2 Tell Sr. A. Natalina: the Mother has written and told me to send you to Pistoia with Sr. A. Emma.

Tell me something about the sick sisters; for pity's sake do not send any of them, keep them all with you. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

She is unwell and about to leave for Naples. She asks for prayers.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. A line in haste, because I am about to leave for Naples and have had a fever for two days. 1 I hope you received my letter asking you to accept the postulants and keep the money yourself, and many other things.2

  2. Goodbye; pray for me that I may recover and make the journey with less suffering.

Goodbye, yours for all ages affectionate M. Rosa

Advice about her brother Checco. She approves everything she has done.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am about to leave. Three days ago I wrote to your mother to have Checco's application made at once, and I want them to do it at once as I told her. Meanwhile, keep pressing.1 By the 18th of this month he will have notice of where to report, and if this time they do not respond and do it, woe betide them!

  2. As for what you tell me, all is well. Courage! The days pass quickly and so I shall return.

  3. Today a postulant will have arrived bringing £ 250; give a hundred to Gaspare, and if [others] come give him another 300. Do you understand? I am delighted with what you do and how you act. Well done!2

  4. How is it you tell me you were some days without letters from me, when I always write?

  5. You did very well not to send the money to Sr. A. Santina,3 no, she should have asked me; you always have a safeguard in saying that (if I do not) you cannot without my consent.4

  6. For your information, tomorrow I leave for Naples; I will try to finish as quickly as I can.

Goodbye. Greetings to Beppa and to you; believe me yours affectionate M. Rosa

She cannot come to her at once: she was ill the day before and must go to Naples urgently. She will return soon.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. I am very sorry I cannot come,1 because of the bad weather and the fever that kept me in bed yesterday, and since tomorrow I must leave for Naples, which [is] really urgent; but I promise that on my return I will come to you, have no doubt.2

  2. I shall stay there only briefly, as little as I can. Keep your spirits up; do not be upset.

Goodbye, yours for all ages, affectionate M. Rosa

She authorises her to go collecting alms. She approves what she has done. She will send more Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I cannot understand how you say you did not receive my letter telling you to go collecting alms with Sr. A. Maurina.1 Yes, go. I am sorry, for it was a long letter in which I told you many things. Enough.

  2. All you have done is good;2 courage, always forward, always in the Lord's presence.

  3. And as soon as I can I will send you sisters; I have already given orders and hope they will send you some.

  1. I am about to leave for Naples and extremely busy.3

Goodbye; greetings to the Sisters, and thank them for their letters. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

Let her take care to balance service to the sick with observance and the Sisters' real capacities. News and advice.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear you are doing a great many night watches; this displeases me, and I tell you I do not want it, for if you sit up nights, I tell you, you cannot and I do not want it; so you will always be at home and able to supervise.2

  2. And then, how can observance be kept? This first, and then you will have everything, if observance is in your House.3

  3. The world was made little by little, and when the sick cannot be accepted they are not accepted, for it is better to send them away than to do more than your strength allows.4

  4. Tell the relatives of that Sister of ours to be patient; I will let them see her this summer, for now it is impossible; this summer they will give the money and I will have her accompanied, but not now.5

  5. So accept the postulant and put her in the kitchen, and you will see she will do well.6 At the end of April I will have two more sent to you, so they will be useful; for now a little patience is needed!

  6. Be cheerful and strong in health, and let us try to do everything for Jesus. Greetings to all the sisters; God bless them all; and I am

your affectionate M. Rosa

She is tired, has much work and longs to return.

Dearest children,

1. Sr. A. Benedetta is handing me the letter so that I can add a couple of lines.1 What shall I tell you? That I am very tired; so much work! Dear children, you long for me, but I long to return. I am always trying to get things done quickly; I always put everything aside for the dear little girls.2

Goodbye. Affectionate greetings, and I am

Your affectionate M. Rosa

Directions and advice about a novice, the postulants and the running of the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear all you tell me about Sr. A. Serafina, all of it; so take Sr. A. Serafina out of the novitiate and from under the obedience of that unfortunate woman. Oh! what a hard character!1

  2. Checco is going to Alessandria for his examinations. Let us hope all goes well; I have just sent mamma a letter I received from Rome; I assure you one could not wish for more!2

  3. If the postulant arrives with 2000, do not spend it; first we must see whether she stays, for it would be a problem.3 Listen, I return the postulant's letter; accept her. I hope you have already accepted the teacher; we need her.

  4. You did well to bake bread at home; it will be a saving. Find out the price of wheat; ask Count Camillo and then write to me, and we will buy a little,4 but only a little, for it keeps falling and, thank God, we shall have a fine harvest!

I end because I am really in a hurry; I am yours for ever, affectionate M. Rosa

She thanks her for the prayers. She is better. She asks for news of the Sisters sent to her community. All she has done is good.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Thanks to your prayers I am on my feet and can do my duty well enough. Thank you, then!1 My head is not tormenting me, so I can write with less effort.

  2. Now to practical matters: the sisters have arrived; are they useful to you? are they doing well? watch their tongues!2 Otherwise all is well.

  3. Courage; if you think you should go to Pisa, go and please Angiolina.3 As for the postulants, all is well; I will do my best to pass through Pistoia.4 Be cheerful and believe me, in haste,

your affectionate M. Rosa

She has done everything well in accepting the postulants and she approves it all. On her return they will meet in Piacenza, have no doubt.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Your letter, which I have just finished reading:1 I see you always fear you are not doing well;2 put that fear aside and act with confidence! Well done! Courage! Everything done well about the postulants; I approve it all.

  2. As for your not being there when I arrive, will you be? for, in all confidence and secrecy, I shall not be able to be in Piacenza before early June, God willing, so that I can work continuously as I did, without interruption.

  3. So, about the Sisters to be sent, I did not quite understand; do what you think best, but at once, for at Lodi they need them badly.3

Goodbye, in haste your affectionate M. Rosa

She explains how to proceed to collect an inheritance. Let her wait for a copy of the will.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear from your letter of the inheritance you have received, but I do not want you to give anyone power of attorney;1 go to Genoa, see that you leave nothing to anyone and take good advice;2 before signing I would like you to send me a copy of the will, so that I can tell you what to do.

  2. Say that you can do nothing, because, as the goods are not yours,3 you cannot dispose of anything given your vow, and before signing and deciding you are bound, under penalty, to refer to the Mother;4 and moreover that these goods were left with the intention of serving the Community.

  3. So set off and send me a copy of the will at once, and then I will reply, for I can also use the telegraph. On my way back from Rome I am coming to Florence, because I need to stop at Pistoia. For your information I shall be there in early June.

Goodbye; greetings to all, and believe me your affectionate M. Rosa

She fears letters are going astray. She is pleased with the good news of the Sisters. Let her not worry about the Sunday Masses; she will settle it on her return. She will bring a postulant with her.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I gather from your little note received yesterday2 that you are without our letters; can it be? when I wrote a few hours before leaving and then as soon as I arrived. Can they be going astray?

  2. I would like to know whether Onorata has received my letter, because, seeing no reply to the many things I asked her — indeed two letters, one from Rome and the other from here — I am worried they are going astray. Now I shall not write for 3 days, as I am going to Giugliano and will be back on Friday.3

  3. You ask about the Sisters who want to go to the Bishop with the postulant: take them yourself and do not leave them; a brief visit and then away; greet him for me.4 I assure you the good news of the Sisters is a great consolation to me.

  4. I am sending this letter back to you; accept the two postulants on the terms stated in it.

  5. As for the Sunday Masses, tell the Chaplain that when I arrive I will settle them myself, for the story is too long to tell!5

  6. I hope you will put a chain on Beppina and not let her go away;6 for pity's sake let her wait for me; I will come with a dear little Countess who will later become a nun; she is already with me.

In 20 days a beautiful piano will reach you, but you must not give away the one there, no; the one arriving belongs to this girl, who plays very well. Tell Carla, so she will be pleased, and Beppa. Goodbye, I am overwhelmed with work! Goodbye

your affectionate M. Rosa

My head always aches!

Advice about a Sister and the house.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. From the telegram you will have seen I did not want you to send Sr. A. Natalina.23 "My God! Do not trust her; keep her well watched, for she will stir up gossip, and I want to know always how she behaves, both she and the other, for otherwise painful steps will have to be taken; do you understand me?

  2. You must not leave them long in those cloisters;4 try to change them, and I hope you went with them yourself.

  3. Otherwise everything you have done is fine; if the two Sisters have arrived, you can also use these two to relieve the other two after 10 or 8 days;5 not longer, I think, for I have tried others already, and they soon get used to that very monotonous life.6

  4. So be careful; I enclose a line for Sr. A. Liberata, which you will give her. Goodbye; greetings to all; I am

your affectionate M. Rosa

She forbids her to do night watches with the sick. She asks for reports on the Pisa house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. In a spare moment I answer yours, which I received yesterday in Naples.1 I hear you are doing night watches; I absolutely do not want it, for you no longer have the strength for such exertion.

  2. How can you tell me you left the poor Canon alone? Oh! That is too much; what if he were taken ill? No, no, such things will not do; they are imprudent.2

  3. So you tell me you are 14 — how so? You must be fifteen, surely?3 Enough; this letter will find you already back from Pisa, so you can write and tell me how that house is going.

I shall be there in early June. Greetings to all, and believe me your affectionate M. Rosa. Tomorrow I shall be in Naples.

She has much work and is unwell. She asks her to go to Pisa for two days.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am so overwhelmed with work that I do not know how to manage it all; besides, my headache torments me and I assure you I cannot [...] Enough!1

  2. You should go to Pisa for at least two days; I assure you it is my wish,2 and then straight back to Pistoia. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

Permission to go collecting alms.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just one line; be patient, for when I come I will settle everything! When you have to go collecting alms,1 take whomever you think best; I have no time to answer everything, as I am immensely busy.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me your affectionate M. Rosa

Let her not accept the postulant of "advanced age"; the others, yes.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. In great haste, for I am overwhelmed with work. Listen, the old postulant you mention cannot be accepted, no, because of her age;1 otherwise all is well; the other young ones, yes.

  2. The Father who succeeded Father Olivieri — you can tell Marchioness Anguissola, for she knows him, since she gives him alms.2

Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

She has asked the Holy Father's blessing for him and his brother. She has received the other birth certificate and will send it.

Most worthy Count,

  1. I have not written again because I kept waiting for the certificates of the two, so as to tell you everything at once.1

  2. So first I will tell you that I received from the Holy Father a special blessing for you and your brother;2 he received me kindly and in his goodness had me sit down. How good he is! to me, so wretched and unworthy a creature!

  3. Now in Naples I am in a sea of business, but always thinking of you and eager for news of you and your eyes. Sr. A. Battistina has shown me a keen wish to know how you are, and the day before yesterday, when I was with her,3 we often exclaimed: "Oh! If the Counts were here, how they would enjoy themselves! Come! Come!

  4. Yesterday at last I received another certificate. You will see that this one too has the father, or the mother, living, but rest assured they can do no harm, for they would sooner benefit than diminish or appropriate; then it is enough to say that he is the Father's brother, and I think that suffices.4

  5. I will send you the other later, because there was a mistake and the one I have is not right.5 My God! What it takes to get anything from town councils! Write and tell me how you are, or have someone write.

Greet your brother, Father Cirillo and Don Luigi. Believe me ever your affectionate Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

She explains how to deal with two Sisters who will arrive at the Mother House.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. A line in haste. Listen, at Arena Po a sister has fallen ill and they need another. See whether you have one to send;1 you could take her yourself, couldn't you? so as not to let her go alone, since you are going anyway.2

  2. Listen, Sr. A. Matilde will come to you; treat her well;3 tell her I will soon have her study; then, with kindness, you will rid her of all the crooked ideas she has, and she will get back on the right path. Take great care that she does not write to her sister secretly, I beg you.

  3. Listen, Sr. A. Salvatore will come to you; send her straight on to Pistoia, where she will find my orders as to where she must go; for pity's sake send her as soon as she arrives. If money has come, give her about 100.4 And as soon as you can, give Gaspare 300 for the interest he has to pay.

  4. I hope postulants have arrived; tell me how many there are and whether you expect more.5

Goodbye, yours for ever affectionate M. Rosa

She may accept the postulant. Advice about her sister Giuseppina. She asks for the printed form of the Clothing rite.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Tell the postulant you will receive her with the extra 200.1 Send Sr. A. Nazzarena at once to Lodi, where they need a cook.2

  2. As for Giuseppina, if she comes with the Marchioness, remember it is very hot here and dress her modestly;3 not one of the hats she has, no, you know, modest ones like caps of that sort, for here you see nothing else. If she needs anything, buy it without saying a word; get her what she needs to be modest. Goodbye

your affectionate M. Rosa

3. Send me one of the sheets used [for] the clothing ceremony;4they are in the last pigeonhole where the newspapers are, the same as the one you know is used for clothing!

She has received her letters. She reminds her to put into practice the advice given before her departure. She encourages her and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received the two letters; in one I found a little fear and heard of you at Pistoia;1 in the other I see you are happier and no longer so fearful, and likewise about the good Parish Priest.2

  2. For pity's sake do not forget to put into practice the advice I gave you before leaving; what can I do? I am always wary of writing, because...

  3. So courage, we shall soon see each other.3 Pray and have others pray; tell the dear Sisters. I should also tell you that I shall not be back before mid-June, so there is time.

Goodbye; greetings to all, and a thousand good wishes to you in the Heart of Jesus; I am your affectionate M. Rosa

Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi will come to Pistoia to collect three Sisters. If possible let her pay their journey to Naples, or at least to Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear from your letter that you have not gone to Pisa; if you think you should go, I leave you free.1

  2. Now pay attention: Sr. A. Salvatore will come; give her Sr. A. Norberta and both of those who came from Piacenza, the latest ones though;2 remember they must do night watches and are needed for Naples. For pity's sake do not send me old ones3, no; I always mean novices, and Sr. A. Norberta; do you understand?4

  3. For pity's sake I beg you; only, if you could give them the money to get here, you would do me a great favour; I have written to the Superior of Piacenza to give £ 700 if she had it, but fearing she may not, if you could, she will repay you as soon as she has it, for they are needed to open a House in Palermo, and they are to give me the travel money.5

  4. So see what you can do; if you cannot, telegraph me and tell me what you are doing, whether you can give them at least as far as Rome, and from there I will try to turn to Brother Agostino.6 If you do not have the 100 [f.], you can give them the fare to Rome.

  5. We will do this: give the enclosed to Sr. A. Salvatore. Goodbye, thank you for the prayers; thank the Sisters for me and give them my love; and you receive a big7

affection from your M. R.

She asks her to submit the application for reduced fares on the Southern Railways.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. The day before yesterday I learnt that the Sisters of St Vincent had the good fortune to obtain half-price tickets on the Southern line,1 and what about us? See what you can do; go and enquire, with that fine opportunity you have;2 do not delay; they tell me one must apply to the Ministry.

  2. Listen: if the Superior is not there, you do it, dear Eletta; send for that gentleman.3 Goodbye, yours for ever

affectionate M. Rosa

Fr Tornatore has invited Marchioness Anguissola to Naples. Let her go to her to hear her instructions and wishes.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. It is late and I am tired, but I must write all the same; so, in strict secrecy: the Father has written to the Marchioness to come to Naples and to take Giuseppina as her companion.1 So you can go to her and say: the Father (says) sent word that I should come to you to receive your orders and do as you tell me, including about the companion for Naples; and nothing more.2 See whether she says yes; then be sure to give Giuseppina some money so that she can buy anything she needs for the journey; I think they will stop in Florence and Rome; give them food.3 She pays for the whole journey; I mean the Marchioness pays for both.

1. Another worry! as if I did not have enough!4 My God! Let us leave that! Do you know anything about Checco?5

Goodbye, yours for ever,

affectionate M. Rosa

She is pleased with her service at Pisa. She will return at the end of the month. Advice. News of her own health.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours and hear many things about Pisa. Well done, my dear little lamb!1 I also received your telegram.

  2. You should have taken all the money from the one at Pisa.2 Listen, you can go back on the last day of the month, or for the opening of the Chapel3 I want you to be there; you understand, don't you?

  3. Listen, I have written a million times to that Superior4 to accept the postulant and put her in the kitchen, so she will be useful, won't she? You will do it when you go back, collecting the dowry and keeping it with you.

  4. So one thing I urge you: look after your health and do not eat strofugi.5 Goodbye, I am so busy and tired that my poor head...! pray for me and believe me yours for all ages

affectionate M. Rosa

The two Sisters should sit their certificate examinations at Ravenna. She will send the documents the Sister teacher is waiting for.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Your letter was a real consolation.1 Well done, well done! So tell them they will sit the examinations at Ravenna. Yes, Ravenna will be much better.2

  2. Thank the confessor for me, and a thousand blessings to you.3 Tell Sr. A. Leopoldina that I have written again about her certificate and hope to have everything.4

Goodbye, yours for all ages affectionate M. Rosa

P.S. Tell Sr. A. Leopoldina that I will tell her everything in person and she will be pleased.

Communications and advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Keep knocking again and again about the seats; do not let them sleep on it.1 I return the will;2 you did everything well, well done! As for the Sisters, we shall see when I come! Stand firm about the confessors. Goodbye,

your M. Rosa

Directions on accepting two postulants and on the community. News.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. A line in reply to yours, which I read last night on getting back from Capua at 9,1 and I hear you are afraid you did wrong. No, I tell you that you did everything very well.

  2. So I return the letters; one is not accepted; to the other, the one with a thousand F., reply that you cannot accept her unless she pays at least £ 500 and guarantees a franc a day for her stay, otherwise she should stay at home; the other 500 she will give at profession.

  3. The cobbler Sister,2 for pity's sake do not send her anywhere; indeed, see that she does not do night watches, so we shall have a good cobbler. Do not send anyone there, for Sr. A. Riparata will be well;3 do not worry about the cook; no one is indispensable in God's works!4 Write to me always. On Thursday there is a clothing of 4 here, and others remain whom I will bring when I come. Goodbye. In haste, yours always

affectionate M. Rosa

She is astonished at the Superior's behaviour. Let her instruct her well. Advice and rules for accepting postulants.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Oh! what misguided humility that thoughtless Superior has! What do you say? I assure you I am truly flabbergasted;1 please go for the opening of the house, that is, of the Chapel.2

  2. I hope that by the time you receive this letter the Sisters will have passed through, that is, been sent off.3

  3. So you can go back to Pisa and try to shake that Superior up; tell her this is misguided humility; do all you can to rouse her.4

  4. Listen, as for the postulant, accept her; you could put her in the kitchen if you think fit, otherwise send her to Piacenza, together with the one you accepted.

  5. Listen, those two you tell me about, from the missionary, I am very wary, for they have never given us a good one, and as an excuse they say they do not accept them without a dowry, which is not true at all, for they take poor girls just as we do and worse; but if they have faults, they send them to us!5 See them first, observe them well, make sure they are of legitimate parents, and so step by step, and if you then think them suitable, accept them,6 and send them along with the one from Pisa.

  6. For a cook, see whether you have one; you could take her there. Goodbye, yours for all ages,

affectionate M. Rosa

She encloses the two letters sent to her for review. She is glad the postulants will increase.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Here I am writing again; I forgot to put the two letters in.1

  2. Oh! how glad I was to hear you have real hope of being able to pay the bills! Oh! May God hear you!2

  3. I am glad to hear the postulants will increase. Oh! if only there were 1000\ so there would be a fine clothing. You did well to accept that strong one, and if more come, accept them at once. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

She states her wishes about the area for alms-collecting. She encloses a letter.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear you are undertaking such a long journey for alms-collecting; that would not be my wish; I would like you to stay only in the surrounding area;1 so I am writing at once, and if you are not there they will forward it to you; I will tell you the reason in person.2

  2. For the rest be patient; on my return I will settle everything; it is a time of sacrifice.

God bless you, and believe me your affectionate M. Rosa

Let her drive away melancholy; all she has said and done is good. She would like to tell her many things but has no time.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Your melancholy is nothing but a devilish trick; keep your spirits up; everything you have said and done is excellent!1 God wants to purify us, and to have eternal glory we must suffer.

  2. I would like to tell you so many things, but for lack of time we must be patient; one cannot do what one would like. Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me always

your affectionate M. Rosa

She has had no letters for over a month, which causes her worry and pain. She always remembers her and prays for them all. She awaits news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. It is now a month and more since I received a letter from you. You cannot believe how anxious I am! Are you ill, perhaps? What are they all doing? Then so many thoughts come to me! Why not write? Though I am travelling and under such a burden of business that I have no breathing space, I can say I have missed only one post without writing.1

  2. Sometimes I think: "could my Giuseppina be travelling? Oh! I do not think so, for leaving those people!2 Alas! How will they manage?" What can I tell you? In short, I tell you to write, for pity's sake!

  3. The Sisters have already forgotten their poor Mother, but it is not so with me, for I always pray and can truthfully say that not a morning passes without my praying to the Saint especially for all of you before leaving church. Oh! what are you doing? I want you not to leave me anxious.

  4. Another time I will write at greater length; I am immensely busy, indeed swamped with business, houses to open, visits to Houses!3 Enough.

Pray and be cheerful, and believe me ever, for all ages, yours and all of yours affectionate M. Rosa

Let her send a Sister teacher's documents to Mercatello. Two cases will arrive. She asks for news of some Sisters' conduct.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Listen, try to have Sr. A. Maria's certificate collected from the Inspector,1 and you can tell Onorata to draft the application, and you will copy it out, saying it is to send her to another school for the new year; when you have it, send it to the archpriest at Mercatello with all the documents: birth certificate, etc.

  2. I have bought 5 dozen very fine sets of cutlery with magnificent knives for our refectory; not luxurious but nice, and tomorrow I will send them with other things for you to keep, as well as the case containing a magnificent Madonna. Oh! how beautiful she is! for pity's sake do not touch her; I have already written to Gaspare what to do.

  3. I want to know whether Sr. A. Agnese has arrived. Dear Sr. A. Francesca! See how she is; make sure she writes to no one, neither women nor men; send the letters to me. Be very careful, for pity's sake.2 How is Sr. A. Matilde?3 and has Sr. A. Nazzarena gone? I have just received yours along with Sr. A. Nazzarena's and hear many beautiful things God has worked in that heart.4

  4. Oh! If only the Marchioness did not come! how [fitting] that would be; I hope to leave on Monday or Tuesday, so if she is two days late she will be too late.5 Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

She authorises her to exchange sisters between the Pisa and Pistoia houses. She is unhappy at the praise of herself in the leaflets printed for the opening of the work in Pisa.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Overwhelmed with work, I reply as best I can. Yes, make all the exchanges you think best, for the good of both houses.

  2. A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. It seems to me your demands are unreasonable and uncharitable, for I do not write in my own hand.1 What! I arrived after a long journey, having brought from Naples an inflammation that made me very ill in Rome and then in Florence; and not only that, but always with a mountain of business on my back. On arriving here I was in bed for many days; true, I worked all the time lying down, but my God! One can imagine how much has piled up! so much that I have not yet been able to deal with it all,2 and how could I stop to write to you, when it is about trifles and I have seen and spoken with you! oh! come! let us be a little serious and sensible, and not demand what cannot be had.3

2. Otherwise you did well to go to the Archbishop, but I always see things done with little sense. Why did you not first find out whether the Archbishop was there or not? A wasted journey, money thrown away for nothing.4 I would like things done more sensibly.

3. Nor do I see any great disgrace if that teacher says we are not approved. Oh! let her say what she likes! Did they not speak against Our Lord? And was it only trifles like these?5 Oh! far from it! Do you know what you must do? Strive to be observant, do your duty and give good example: that is your defence, and I would have you do nothing else.

4. If you do this, God will vindicate you by giving you fine consolations. If you seek vindication yourselves, oh! how unbecoming for a Daughter of Saint Anne. Oh! this is not my spirit, dear daughters, no; for thousands of times by God's mercy I was ...6 but! never! did I dare open my mouth; they were made too dear to me; so must it be with you. Let Sr. A. Sempliciana hear this too, if you think fit, if you like.

Goodbye, yours for ever affectionate M. ROSA

She has received four letters. She urges her not to overwork and not to be upset by the sisters' complaints. She should look after everyone's health. She is waiting for the money to send the Sisters. She approves the printing of the Rules and prayer books in Spanish.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. The day before yesterday I received four letters from you. They must have been held up somewhere: one was of 4 April, one of 27 March, another of 8 April and another of 22 April — see how they do things!

2. I hope the fighting is over and you have nothing more to fear.1 Please do not overwork; take on servants, accept postulants and let them do the work, and spare the sisters, so they will not be so tired.2

3. In the last one you seem so upset that I feel for you. I would like you to take things calmly, for grumbling is calmed by patience and by doing or giving some penance. Cheer up: I am writing, and I hope everything will have changed by now.3

4. Above all I urge you to look after yourself and the sisters. Spare nothing for your health; so courage!

5. I hope you have received my letters asking you to send me some of the Americans, and I will send you the sisters you mention; and I would like the benefactor to send me the money to send you more Sisters, for you are too few and cannot hold out.4 So have the money sent to me and I will send the sisters at once, for I fear that being so few you will suffer. I hear you are wearing yourself out. So take care of yourself; please do not get up too early, and eat more.

6. Tell me, is there no more news of those two hospitals?5 Oh! How good it would be if the sisters were called to other Cities! I cannot understand: the contract says that if sisters die others will be requested, so why do they not do so?6

7. Enough; let us turn to your last letter,7 in which I see you are distressed over nothing, since there is nothing serious, only little silliness; the grumbling will end; cheer up and do not fret, for I hope that by the time mine arrive everything will be nicely settled. Do not be upset.

8. You did well to have the rules printed in Spanish. I hope there are only a few copies, so that if there is anything — mind, nothing is to be added for now; if so you will be told.8 The books too; well done; the Spanish Novices will be able to read and learn them.9

9. If the sisters come, it is good that they bring everything themselves, for otherwise too much10 would be seen; it is not wise to trust others, but to do everything ourselves, isn't it? The less people know the better. I will not speak of my health, for I am really unwell and weak, but that comes from the great strain of three months travelling about.11

Goodbye, yours for all ages affectionate M. ROSA

My daughter,

1. You cannot imagine how comforted I was to hear how united you are. Oh! Blessed Charity! Well done, daughter! May God pour His choicest blessings on your head.1

2. You are quite right about the sick sister; I had already written so to her,2 but two things always happen when nothing more can be done for a sister: first, superiors try to get her off their hands quickly, don't they? am I right? Not all, but! What do you say? and second, the doctor, prompted by the superior, at once prescribes a change of air.

your affectionate M. ROSA

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. I cannot find words worthy enough to thank Your Most Reverend Excellency, as I would wish, for all the effort and interest you are showing in having the poor Daughters of Saint Anne there.2

2. Truly we do not deserve such charity, whose reward we leave in the hands of Him who can do all things and will justly repay it. For our part, we can only show our gratitude by assuring you of our prompt obedience and filial, respectful attachment, should we have the good fortune to be counted among your children, and of the exact fulfilment of our duties, so that Your Most Reverend Excellency may never regret having worked so hard to call us to Sarsina.3

3. I accept your proposal and undertake to send the five sisters with the qualifications you mention, for an annual payment of 1500 lire. Your Most Reverend Excellency and the Honourable Mayor also recognise how small this stipend is, but I ask no increase, trusting that it will be made up by Your Excellency's valued support and by the good people there, in whom we place our trust.4

4. The poor sisters will be entrusted to you as to a father, and I am sure they will always find help and protection from Your Most Reverend Excellency.

5. I have sent the Mayor there 5 a letter framed in the terms you outlined. The boarding school can be discussed later.5

I renew my thanks to Your Most Reverend Excellency and, prostrate at your feet, ask your pastoral blessing.

Most humble Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. ' I am delighted to hear that the sisters enjoy perfect health; this is in reply to yours of 24 January last. Oh!

what a distance, my God!1

2. I do not know how you never receive my letters, in which I told you to send me Sister Anna Clelia and two or three of those novices; since you have found so good a gentleman who helps you generously, take advantage of it and send me the Sisters and the money, for that way they would be safe. So hasten their departure.2

3. I keep hearing that I should prepare the sisters for you. It has been a good month and nothing is to be seen, so one does not know what to do. Until I receive the money to send them, I will not gather them together, for it would be a waste [of] time.3

4. I cannot tell you how much I have to do, my God! And always my head aching, almost continuously. My God! How sweet is suffering! I assure you I have plenty; what am I saying! It is never enough, for it is always great and beautiful and sweet!4 Oh! Daughter, how many there are — an abyss!

5. My dearest daughter, if God grants me life to see each other, oh! then you would see whether America is here too! I say Italy is a real uproar beyond understanding, a confusion of minds!5 Enough.

6. Let us accept everything and make it count, so that there may be a discount on our sins, which we always need to purge!6

7. As for the Sisters, stand firm: one confessor and one extraordinary confessor, nothing more, for so our order and Holy Rules require. Listen, have no fear about Father R.7 Observance and again observance, sacrifice of ourselves, and then fear nothing even if all hell rose up; fear not, for you will always be victorious and not a hair of your head will be lost. So always strong, without fear. Let us keep our prow always turned towards the Lord and the boat will never strike the rocks; for the prow is our mind, and if we keep it always turned to Him and do everything in His presence, there is no doubt that nothing will go wrong, but everything must always turn out well.8

8. In everything I have acted for Your glory and honour, my God, my only thought, my support, my life, my every action.

9. This is what your poor Mother tries to do: she breathes only for Jesus, has no thought but for Jesus; everyone strikes and vies to beat me, but I always carry the banner victorious. Not I, but Jesus who conquers, and victorious in Him.9 Oh! sweet Love! Love and do everything for Jesus; believe me

My daughter,

I am registering this one1 and mean to send it to someone from whom I hope you can get them, and I enclose one for all the sisters, which I want you to give them at once without even appearing curious to read them.2 I am quite sure of your obedience.

2. Now let me repeat what I have always written: it is not advisable to send anyone from here, but you must do this. You can send me two or three of the Americans you have clothed together with Sr. A. Clelia, and they can quite well travel by themselves.3 There are always people coming; you could put them together. So I really want to see them; then I will see to sending you the number you need.

3. Oh! How it grieves me to be always without your letters; I always go one or two months without receiving any. What do you think? You tell me the war is now over.4

4. As for sending the sisters, you should take advantage of your protector's good intentions, so that he would bear the cost.5

5. I will not speak of the needs of the house, for they are beyond compare! My God! What sorrow! If God wills, He will leave me in this world, ill as I am, and then I will have the good fortune to see you; with God's help keep yourself healthy and strong so that you can return when you see everything well settled.

6. Please write; I cannot wait for other houses to be opened, so that by moving the sisters about a little6 they are better off and do their work well. Goodbye, I am yours for all ages affectionate M. ROSA

May Jesus always hold you close to His heart.

My daughter,

1. Your letter tells me such lovely things that I am truly comforted, and about Sr. A. Zeale too, to whom I have written.1 I hope she has received it and will no longer say I do not write to her.

2. Believe me, every time you write I write to you; I am not answering this one of Sr. A. Zeale's, because I wrote to her two days ago, having replied two days ago.2

4. For pity's sake, always be steadfast in loving Jesus alone; close your heart to every earthly affection, but keep it wide open and loving to possess that of Jesus; I wish you to be consumed in Him and for Him. Love Mary and she will give you Jesus. I am yours, affectionate M. ROSA

Tell the others I will write before the month is out.

My daughter,

1. I am replying rather late, but I am so overwhelmed with work. First let me tell you that your friend is no longer to be seen; then I hear of your troubles. Listen, my dear, suffering for Jesus is a very precious thing. Ah! blessed are you, for your sufferings united to sacrifice will one day be your great joy. Listen, all that is pain will one day be joy!2

2. One thing only you must do: try to flee from grumbling.3 Ah! Infernal monster, which does our souls such harm!

3. After embracing so beautiful a mission, to think that this monster comes to disfigure it, ah! how dreadful!4

4. Stand firm, my dears, for the infernal dragon is roaring against you because he sees you have gone to steal souls, and so he is furious and tries all his infernal wiles to see whether he can at least disturb you and make you lose your peace. No! You shall not win!

5. The Holy Mother protects you and St Michael the Archangel defends you. I commend devotion to this Saint to you. 6. Goodbye; greetings to you both, sisters,5 for I have written this to both of you. Pray for me as I always pray for you, and stay always close to the Heart of Jesus, where every day I embrace you and hold you tight in Him; I am ever

your affectionate M. ROSA

My daughter,

1. I have received yours dated 1 August. Oh! How pleased I was, what comfort it brought me! God bless you a thousand times! Oh! If you could send what you say you have, it would truly be a great good and relieve me of so many worries and anxieties!1

2. As for the fur you mention,2 instead of sending it to the Bishop you could send it to the Cardinal Protector, who does so much for us; I hope you have received the copy of the letter and have already sent it to him, haven't you?3

Cunegonda instead, if you think it right, can't you? For pity's sake send me something. Oh! If only I could have it all.5

6. So let us trust in Him alone and work for Him alone; for pity's sake do not worry about anything; be cheerful; let all the crosses and tribulations be mine! Oh! how many there are, dear daughter, if you only knew.7

7. You know, even Fr Accinelli has turned against me, and why? Because he quarrelled with a Superior and then 7 Oh! how many I still have to see!!! Enough.

8. For Jesus all is little; so think of one who is on the cross, full of longing to die on it. Goodbye. I am yours for all ages

affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. Greetings to all the Sisters and especially to the American Novices, whom I have not yet had the good fortune to meet; I want them all to pray for me, for I need it so much. Goodbye.

1. I have just received your esteemed letter of the 12th, to which I reply promptly.

2. Probably in my letter of the day before yesterday I did not explain my intentions to you, or did not do so clearly enough for you to understand me.2

3. I therefore repeat now what I meant to convey in that letter, namely that I accept the proposal made to this Institute3 regarding the Pious Hospice of Saint Anne, on whatever terms and conditions the Honourable Commission that administers it, of which you are President, may set.

4. I should also have been glad to know the conditions offered by the Religious who have put themselves forward to you.4

5. I trust that after this letter there will be no further obstacle and that you will be able to conclude this negotiation with your customary kindness and courtesy;5 for this, I repeat, I shall always be most grateful, and I shall seek an early opportunity to express my gratitude in person rather than in writing.

With all respect I remain

Your most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She informs her of some Sisters' transfers and asks her to come to Piacenza.1

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You would need to arrange to send Sr. A. Estella to Invorio and take back Sr. A. Donata. See in your wisdom how you could have Sr. A. Beata accompany them; what do you think? It will be too costly, won't it? Do you want me to send you the money?2 but this change really is necessary; anyway, as soon as she is back we will think about it.3 Oh! wretched girl, it is time to put an end to this, for we really must clean house, mustn't we?4

2. So send me Sr. A. Dorotea at once; if you bring her yourself I will be pleased, for I would not want her to come alone.5

3. I am sending you this Sister so that the Doctor may cure her; she has a fever, but nothing much, yet here I see the poor thing never gets better! What a pity, so strong and good a young woman! Send her back as soon as she is well.

4. If before sending Sr. A. Estella you brought me Sr. A. Dorotea I would be better pleased, for we could arrange things differently; what do you think?6 So I expect you tomorrow with Sr. A. Dorotea. Goodbye your affectionate M. ROSA

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. As soon as you receive this, send Sr. A. Guglielma to Piacenza at once; I enclose her letter of obedience. Please send her straight away.2 Nothing more for now. In haste, yours in my dear Crucified,

Advice for the teacher who wishes to become a religious. She is grieved at some Sisters' conduct.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have just received your registered letter with the teacher's inside. Oh! how pleased I was! Listen, tell the teacher I am delighted she should go home for the holidays, and meanwhile I think she should speak to her family in person about becoming a nun, for in writing it does not seem suitable.1 And let her tell them that as long as her father lives I will always give him 15, even something more, but she should tell him herself.2

2. Oh! daughter, if it were really true? would it not be a miracle?

3. Now to those bad ones. First of all you will have seen my telegram and already sent the two to Invorio, haven't you? As for these, I will see to them myself: either I will come or send someone to put an end to it.3

4. I assure you I am deeply grieved; give them the enclosed letter, and read it yourself. Ah! the worst wickedness! what could be more monstrous4 than to rebel against Holy Obedience; I assure you I am truly grieved, and these are the things that pierce my soul! I eagerly await the teacher. Goodbye, courage!

Your affectionate M. ROSA

My daughter,

Be detached from everything, everything.2

Words of encouragement and affection. She gives her view on accepting two postulants.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you tell me. Oh! cursed envy! so much harm! Enough.1 God bless you and give you the patience that is truly needed, and I will never cease holding you close to the Heart of Jesus that He may make you a great saint.

3. For the rest pay no attention, be cheerful, and remember that your poor Mother holds you close and calls herself yours for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA
